statement: Which of these shapes can be turned through less than a full turn about its centre to land exactly on itself, but has no line of symmetry?

choices.text: A kite with sides 3 cm, 3 cm, 5 cm and 5 cm
choices.misconception: I mixed up the two kinds of symmetry: a kite has a mirror line but no turning symmetry, and I read it the wrong way round.

choices.text: An isosceles trapezium with parallel sides 3 cm and 5 cm
choices.misconception: I thought a half turn maps an isosceles trapezium onto itself because its two slanted sides are equal.

choices.text: A parallelogram with sides 3 cm and 5 cm and no right angle
A rectangle measuring 3 cm by 5 cm
choices.misconception: I checked that a half turn works and stopped, without checking for mirror lines, which a rectangle has.

choices.text: An equilateral triangle with sides of 5 cm
choices.misconception: I knew a third of a turn maps it onto itself and assumed a shape with turning symmetry cannot also have mirror lines.

hints: Check each shape twice: once for turning, once for folding.
A shape needs to pass the turning test and fail every folding test. Turning symmetry comes from a centre point; line symmetry means folding along a line makes the halves match exactly.
A half turn about the centre maps a parallelogram onto itself, but folding along either diagonal or across the middle never matches its slanted corners.

solutions.reliable: The rectangle and the equilateral triangle have turning symmetry but also mirror lines. The kite and the isosceles trapezium have a mirror line but no turning symmetry. The parallelogram with unequal sides and no right angles is mapped onto itself by a half turn about the point where its diagonals cross, yet no fold matches it: folding along a diagonal fails because the sides are unequal, and folding across the middle fails because the angles are not right angles. The transferable idea: line symmetry and turning symmetry are independent, so test for each one separately.

whyOnTest: Line and rotational symmetry are tested separately at this level, and the parallelogram is the standard shape that has one without the other.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
